All future readings are compared to this baseline to identify changes, because a slight increase in a specific frequency component is far more meaningful than the absolute level alone. Without a baseline, it is difficult to judge whether current readings are normal for that specific machine.

front: What is the purpose of an oil flushing procedure when commissioning new equipment?
back: An oil flush circulates clean oil through the system at high velocity and temperature before the machine is put into service, to remove metal particles from machining, pipe scale, welding slag, and assembly lubricants that contaminate the fresh oil fill. The flush oil is sampled until it meets the target cleanliness level before the machine starts normal operation. Skipping the flush is a common cause of early bearing and pump failure on new installations.

front: How do you interpret a bearing defect frequency in a vibration spectrum?
back: Each rolling element bearing has four characteristic defect frequencies (BPFO, BPFI, BSF, FTF) calculated from its geometry and running speed. If a peak appears in the vibration spectrum at one of these calculated frequencies, it indicates that particular bearing race or rolling element has a developing defect. Sidebands around the defect frequency indicate the defect is more advanced and is being modulated by shaft rotation.

front: What is a borescope used for in equipment inspection?
back: A borescope is a thin, flexible or rigid tube with a camera that lets you see inside engines, gearboxes, and pipes without taking them apart. It helps find cracks, wear, carbon buildup, or foreign objects. This saves time and avoids unnecessary disassembly.

front: How does a stroboscope help inspect rotating equipment while running?
back: A stroboscope flashes a light at the same speed as a rotating part, making it appear frozen in place. This lets you inspect pulleys, couplings, and fans for wobble, cracks, or imbalance while they are still spinning. You adjust the flash rate until the part looks still.

front: Why is laser alignment considered a predictive maintenance tool?
back: Laser alignment measures misalignment precisely, and trending those measurements over time shows if a machine is shifting or settling on its foundation. Catching misalignment early prevents bearing and coupling failures before they cause downtime. This makes it both a corrective and a predictive tool.

front: What do angular wear patterns on a jaw coupling indicate?
back: Uneven wear on one side of the jaw coupling spider indicates angular misalignment between the driver and driven shafts. If all jaws are worn evenly but heavily, the coupling is overloaded or the wrong durometer spider was selected. Identifying the wear pattern guides the correct repair.

front: How does an infrared thermometer monitor bearing temperature in the field?
back: An infrared thermometer reads surface temperature without contact by measuring radiated heat from the bearing housing. A sudden rise above the baseline temperature, typically more than 10 to 15 degrees Celsius, signals a lubrication problem or early bearing damage. You record readings regularly to build a trend.

front: What is an RTD and how is it used for bearing temperature monitoring?
back: An RTD (resistance temperature detector) is a sensor embedded in or bolted to a bearing housing that changes electrical resistance with temperature. It feeds continuous data to a control system or data logger, allowing real-time monitoring and automatic alarms. RTDs are more accurate than thermocouples for this application.

front: What does bearing enveloping analysis detect that overall vibration misses?
back: Enveloping (also called high-frequency demodulation or spike energy) filters out low-frequency machine noise and looks at the high-frequency impact pulses created when a bearing defect strikes a race. These pulses appear long before overall vibration rises, giving early warning of bearing damage. It is one of the most sensitive bearing fault detection methods.

front: Name four items on a gearbox inspection checklist during a shutdown.
back: A standard gearbox inspection checks oil level and condition (colour, smell, particle content), gear tooth contact pattern and wear, bearing end-play and radial clearance, and seal condition for leaks. You also check the breather to confirm it is clean and functional. Any findings are recorded in the equipment history.

front: What is a fishbone diagram and when is it used in root cause analysis?
back: A fishbone diagram (also called Ishikawa or cause-and-effect diagram) organizes possible causes of a failure into categories such as machine, method, material, man, measurement, and environment. The effect (the failure) goes on the right, and branches show potential causes. It is used during a root cause analysis meeting to make sure no cause is overlooked.

front: Explain the 5 Why root cause analysis method with a simple example.
back: The 5 Why method asks why a failure happened, then asks why that answer happened, repeating up to five times until you reach the root cause. For example: bearing failed, why? No grease. Why? Grease gun empty. Why? No reorder process. The root cause is a missing procedure, not just a dry bearing. Fixing the process prevents recurrence.

front: How often should a torque wrench be calibrated and why does it matter?
back: Most manufacturers recommend calibrating torque wrenches every 12 months or after 5,000 cycles, whichever comes first. An out-of-calibration wrench can under-torque fasteners, causing loosening, or over-torque them, causing fatigue failures. Calibration records must be kept to prove maintenance work was done to the correct specification.

front: How does a desiccant breather prevent lubrication contamination in a gearbox?
back: As a gearbox heats and cools, it breathes air in and out through its breather. A desiccant breather contains silica gel and a filter that remove moisture and particulates from the incoming air before they reach the oil. This is one of the most cost-effective ways to extend oil and bearing life.

front: What is an oil sampling port and how is it used correctly?
back: An oil sampling port is a dedicated valve fitted to a gearbox or reservoir that lets you draw a mid-stream oil sample without shutting down or opening the case. Samples are taken with a clean syringe or pump at the same location and operating temperature every time for consistent trending. The sample is sent to a lab for wear metal, viscosity, and contamination analysis.

front: What are the three types of triggers that can start a planned maintenance interval?
back: Planned maintenance intervals can be triggered by time (calendar-based, such as every 90 days), by usage (hours-based, such as every 2,000 operating hours), or by condition (condition-based, such as when vibration exceeds a set threshold). Most industrial PM programs use a combination of all three triggers depending on the equipment criticality.

front: What does OEE stand for and what does it measure?
back: OEE stands for Overall Equipment Effectiveness. It combines three factors: availability (was the machine running when needed?), performance (was it running at full speed?), and quality (was it producing good parts?). Multiplying all three gives a single percentage that shows how efficiently equipment is being used.

front: How is equipment availability calculated as a maintenance metric?
back: Availability equals uptime divided by total planned operating time, expressed as a percentage. For example, if a machine was planned to run 40 hours but was down for 4 hours, availability is 90 percent. Tracking availability over time shows whether maintenance work is improving or allowing decline in reliability.

front: What does a portable vibration analyzer measure and what data does it collect?
back: A portable vibration analyzer uses an accelerometer held or mounted on a bearing housing to measure vibration amplitude and frequency. It collects overall vibration levels, spectrum data (FFT), and time waveform signals. This data is compared to baseline readings and alarm limits to identify faults such as imbalance, misalignment, looseness, or bearing damage.

front: How does an ultrasound gun detect early bearing faults and air leaks?
back: An ultrasound gun detects high-frequency sound (typically 20 to 100 kHz) that is inaudible to the human ear. A failing bearing produces a distinctive crackling or rushing sound at these frequencies well before any temperature rise or low-frequency vibration change. The same tool finds compressed air and steam leaks by detecting the ultrasound they emit.

front: What does an infrared camera show during electrical and mechanical inspections?
back: An infrared camera creates a thermal image showing temperature differences across a surface. In electrical inspections, hot spots indicate loose connections or overloaded components. In mechanical inspections, a hot bearing housing or overheating coupling shows up as a bright area, allowing the problem to be found without shutting down the equipment.

front: What is a predictive maintenance database used for in a mill or plant?
back: A predictive maintenance database stores equipment readings (vibration, temperature, oil analysis results) over time so trends can be identified. When a reading drifts from its historical normal range, it triggers an alert before failure occurs. The database also stores baseline readings taken on new or freshly rebuilt equipment.

front: Why is trending data more useful than a single vibration reading?
back: A single reading only tells you the current state. Trending compares readings over weeks or months to show whether a machine is getting better, staying stable, or slowly getting worse. A gradual rise in vibration over several months points to developing imbalance or bearing wear, allowing maintenance to be scheduled before breakdown.

front: What information should be recorded in an equipment history file?
back: Equipment history records should include every maintenance action performed, the date and who did it, parts replaced (brand, model, lot number), lubricants added (type and quantity), vibration and temperature readings, and any failures or findings. This history is what makes root cause analysis possible and helps justify capital replacement decisions.

front: What coupling wear pattern indicates parallel (offset) misalignment?
back: Parallel misalignment causes wear across the full width of both coupling hubs but concentrated on opposite sides when the two hubs are compared. In a gear coupling, the gear teeth show wear on one flank only. In a jaw coupling, all spider legs wear but one side of the bore shows more loading.

front: What vibration frequency signature indicates mechanical looseness on an FFT spectrum?
back: Mechanical looseness (such as a loose bearing housing or foot) appears as a series of harmonics at 1X, 2X, 3X, and higher multiples of running speed on the FFT spectrum. The pattern often has many peaks and can look like a forest of lines. Phase analysis can confirm looseness by checking for unstable phase readings.

front: What is the difference between failure mode and root cause in RCA?
back: The failure mode is the way the component failed, for example a bearing inner race crack. The root cause is the underlying reason it happened, such as inadequate lubrication due to a clogged grease line. Fixing only the failure mode (replacing the bearing) without fixing the root cause means the same failure will repeat.

front: What does MTBF mean and how is it calculated?
back: MTBF stands for Mean Time Between Failures. It is calculated by dividing total operating time by the number of failures in that period. For example, if a pump ran 4,000 hours and failed 4 times, MTBF is 1,000 hours. A rising MTBF means reliability is improving; a falling MTBF signals a problem.

front: What is the purpose of an oil cleanliness code (ISO 4406) in a lubrication program?
back: ISO 4406 counts the number of particles per millilitre in oil at three sizes (4, 6, and 14 microns) and assigns a three-number code such as 18/16/13. Cleaner oil has lower code numbers. Hydraulic systems and precision gearboxes require specific cleanliness levels, and lab analysis confirms whether those targets are being met.

front: How does spectrographic oil analysis detect internal machine wear?
back: Spectrographic analysis measures the concentration of metal particles dissolved or suspended in the oil sample, reported in parts per million. Rising iron indicates steel wear, rising copper points to bronze bushings or thrust washers, and rising lead suggests babbit or bearing overlay wear. Trending these numbers over multiple samples shows whether wear is normal or accelerating.

front: What is a P-F curve and how does it guide maintenance scheduling?
back: The P-F curve shows the timeline between the point where a potential failure (P) becomes detectable and the point of functional failure (F). The gap between P and F is the P-F interval. Condition monitoring tools such as vibration analysis or oil sampling must be used at intervals shorter than the P-F interval to catch the fault in time to plan repairs.

front: What is a criticality ranking and why does it affect PM frequency?
back: Criticality ranking scores equipment based on the consequence of its failure: safety risk, production loss, repair cost, and availability of a spare. High-criticality equipment (such as the only pump feeding a process line) gets more frequent inspections and more thorough PM tasks. Low-criticality equipment with an easy-to-replace spare may only need calendar-based checks.

front: How do you convert a fraction like 3/8 to a decimal for a measurement?
back: Divide the top number (numerator) by the bottom number (denominator): 3 divided by 8 equals 0.375. This is useful when a drawing calls out a fractional dimension but your micrometer reads in decimals. Practice the common fractions: 1/4 is 0.250, 1/2 is 0.500, 3/4 is 0.750.

front: What is the ratio and proportion method used for in millwright calculations?
back: Ratio and proportion lets you solve for an unknown when you know three of four related values. For example, if a 20-tooth gear drives a 60-tooth gear and the driver turns at 900 RPM, you set up 20/60 equals x/900 and solve: the driven gear turns at 300 RPM. This method is used constantly for gear ratios, pulley sizes, and flow rates.

front: How do you calculate what percentage one number is of another?
back: Divide the part by the whole, then multiply by 100. For example, if a shaft is 1.998 inches and the nominal size is 2.000 inches, the shaft is 1.998 divided by 2.000 times 100, which equals 99.9 percent of nominal. Percentage calculations are used for efficiency ratings, torque capacity, and load checks.

front: What is the formula for the area of a circle, and where is it used in the trade?
back: Area equals pi times radius squared (A = pi x r squared). You use this when calculating the cross-sectional area of a shaft, pipe bore, or piston to find force, stress, or flow area. For a 4-inch diameter pipe, the radius is 2 inches, so the area is 3.1416 times 2 squared (which equals 3.1416 times 4), giving about 12.57 square inches.

front: How do you calculate the volume of a cylinder such as a hydraulic ram?
back: Volume equals pi times radius squared times length (V = pi x r squared x L). For a hydraulic cylinder with a 3-inch bore and 12-inch stroke, volume is 3.1416 times 1.5 squared times 12, which equals about 84.8 cubic inches. Convert to gallons by dividing by 231 cubic inches per gallon to find oil displacement.

front: How do you convert inches to millimetres for a metric drawing dimension?
back: Multiply inches by 25.4 to get millimetres. For example, 2.500 inches times 25.4 equals 63.5 mm. To go the other way, divide millimetres by 25.4. Keeping a conversion card handy or memorizing that one inch equals 25.4 mm is essential when working from both imperial and metric drawings.

front: How do you convert PSI to kilopascals for a metric pressure specification?
back: Multiply PSI by 6.895 to get kilopascals (kPa). For example, 100 PSI equals 689.5 kPa. To convert back, divide kPa by 6.895. One atmosphere is 14.696 PSI or approximately 101.3 kPa. This conversion comes up when setting relief valves or reading hydraulic specifications written in different unit systems.

front: How do you convert foot-pounds of torque to Newton-metres?
back: Multiply foot-pounds by 1.356 to get Newton-metres (Nm). For example, 100 ft-lb times 1.356 equals 135.6 Nm. To go the other way, divide Nm by 1.356. Torque specifications on modern equipment often appear in both units, and mixing them up is a serious error when torquing fasteners.

front: What is the sine ratio in a right triangle and how is it used for angle work?
back: Sine equals the length of the opposite side divided by the hypotenuse (SOH). A millwright uses this to calculate the rise of an inclined machine base, the height a sling leg reaches above a load, or the offset in a bend. If the angle is 30 degrees, the sine is 0.500, meaning the opposite side is half the hypotenuse.

front: What is the Pythagorean theorem and when does a millwright use it?
back: The Pythagorean theorem states that in a right triangle, the hypotenuse squared equals the sum of the other two sides squared (c squared = a squared + b squared). A millwright uses it to check that a machine base is square (the 3-4-5 method), to find the diagonal of a rectangular layout, or to calculate the length of a diagonal brace.

front: What does orthographic projection show on a mechanical drawing?
back: Orthographic projection shows an object in two or more flat views (front, top, and side) at exactly 90 degrees to each other. Features visible in one view align with the same feature in the adjacent view. A millwright reads these views together to understand the full 3D shape of a part before fabricating or machining it.

front: What is an isometric view on a drawing and when is it used?
back: An isometric view shows a 3D-looking picture of a part or assembly drawn on a flat page with all three axes at 30 degrees to the horizontal. It is used for installation drawings, piping layouts, and assembly guides because it is easier to visualize than multi-view drawings. Dimensions cannot be scaled directly from an isometric view.

front: What does a section view on a drawing reveal about a part?
back: A section view shows what the inside of a part looks like as if it were cut in half and one piece removed. Cross-hatching shows the solid material that was cut through. Section views are used to show internal bores, keyways, wall thickness, and features that would be hidden lines in a standard view.

front: What information is found in a drawing title block?
back: The title block contains the part name and number, the drawing number, the scale, the material specification, the tolerance block (default tolerances if not stated on the drawing), the company name, and the revision level. Always check the title block before reading a drawing to confirm you have the correct and latest version.

front: What does a revision block on a drawing tell you?
back: The revision block lists every change made to the drawing after it was first issued, with a revision letter (A, B, C...), the date of the change, a brief description of what changed, and who approved it. Always use the highest revision level available to avoid working from an outdated drawing.

front: What does a fillet weld symbol on a drawing indicate to a millwright?
back: A fillet weld symbol is a triangle on the reference line of a welding symbol. It tells you the weld is a triangular cross-section bead joining two surfaces at an angle, typically a T-joint or lap joint. The number next to the triangle is the leg size in inches or millimetres, and its position above or below the line indicates which side of the joint gets welded.

front: What does the flatness GD&T symbol control on a machined part?
back: Flatness controls how much a surface can deviate from a perfectly flat plane. The tolerance zone is two parallel flat planes that the entire surface must lie between. It is used for precision machine bases, mounting pads, and split bearing housings where a flat mating surface is critical for proper assembly and alignment.

front: What does the circularity (roundness) GD&T symbol control?
back: Circularity controls how close each cross-section of a round feature is to a perfect circle. The tolerance zone is two concentric circles that every point on the cross-section must fall between. It is important for shaft journals, bearing seats, and cylinder bores where out-of-round surfaces cause uneven loading and premature wear.

front: What is the difference between total runout and circular runout in GD&T?
back: Circular runout measures the variation at each individual cross-section as a shaft is rotated one full turn about a datum axis. Total runout measures the combined effect of all cross-sections and the entire surface simultaneously. Total runout is a tighter, more comprehensive control used for precision rotating parts such as pump impellers and spindles.

front: What is surface roughness Ra and how is it measured?
back: Ra is the arithmetic average roughness, the average height of surface peaks and valleys over a measured length. It is measured with a surface profilometer (contact stylus instrument) in micrometres or microinches. A lower Ra number means a smoother surface. Bearing seats and seal contact surfaces require low Ra values to prevent leaks and premature wear.

front: What is the difference between bilateral and unilateral tolerances on a drawing?
back: A bilateral tolerance allows variation in both directions from nominal, for example 2.000 plus or minus 0.005 (meaning the part can be anywhere from 1.995 to 2.005). A unilateral tolerance allows variation in one direction only, such as 2.000 plus 0.000 minus 0.010. Unilateral tolerances are common on fits where one side of the range is critical.

front: What is the hole basis fit system and why is it preferred in manufacturing?
back: In the hole basis system, the hole is kept at nominal size (the lower deviation of the hole is zero) and the shaft size is varied to achieve the required fit. It is preferred because standard drill and reamer sizes produce consistent holes, making it easier and cheaper to hold the hole at a fixed size than to hold the shaft.

front: What does an ISO fit designation of H7/p6 mean on a drawing?
back: H7 is the hole tolerance: H means hole basis (lower deviation is zero) and 7 is the tolerance grade (IT7). p6 is the shaft tolerance: p means the shaft is oversized relative to the hole (an interference fit) and 6 is the tolerance grade (IT6). H7/p6 is a press fit used for bearing outer rings pressed into housings.

front: What is the difference between a clearance fit and an interference fit?
back: In a clearance fit the shaft is always smaller than the hole, leaving a gap that allows relative motion (used for running fits, sliding fits, and locating fits). In an interference fit the shaft is always larger than the hole, so assembly requires pressing or heating, and the parts hold together by friction (used for press-fit hubs, bushings, and bearing races).

front: How do you read a 0-to-1-inch outside micrometer to the ten-thousandths?
back: Read the sleeve scale (each numbered line is 0.100 inch, each unnumbered line is 0.025 inch), then add the thimble scale (each graduation is 0.001 inch), then add the vernier scale on the sleeve (each graduation is 0.0001 inch). Add all three numbers together. Practicing on a set of standards until readings are repeatable is essential for journeyperson-level work.

front: How do you read a vernier caliper to 0.001 inch?
back: Read the main scale to the last full 0.025-inch increment before the vernier zero line, then find which vernier graduation aligns exactly with a main scale line and multiply that number by 0.001 inch. Add both numbers together. Zero the caliper on a gauge block before critical measurements to confirm it reads correctly.

front: How is a dial bore gauge (telescoping gauge and mic) used to measure a bore?
back: A telescoping gauge is compressed, inserted into the bore at the tightest point, locked, and then withdrawn. The locked dimension is then measured across the gauge pins with an outside micrometer. This two-step process transfers the bore size to the micrometer. Multiple measurements at different depths and angles check taper and out-of-round.

front: What is a dial indicator used for in millwright alignment and assembly work?
back: A dial indicator measures small linear displacements, typically in 0.001-inch increments, by amplifying the movement of a contact point through gears to a needle on a face. Millwrights use it to check shaft runout, coupling face runout, bearing end-play, and to verify alignment corrections during shaft alignment procedures.

front: What is a surface plate used for and how is its accuracy maintained?
back: A granite or cast-iron surface plate provides a reference flat surface for layout, inspection, and precision measurement. Parts are placed on it to check flatness, set up V-blocks, or use height gauges. Accuracy is maintained by keeping it clean, never placing heavy or rough items on it without a soft pad, and having it certified flat on a regular calibration schedule.

front: What is a V-block used for when measuring or inspecting round shafts?
back: A V-block holds a round shaft or bar securely at two contact points so it can be rotated for runout checks with a dial indicator, or held still for layout work. The V angle (usually 90 degrees) centres the round part automatically regardless of diameter within the block's range. V-blocks always come in matched pairs.

front: How is an angle plate used in layout and machining setup work?
back: An angle plate is a precision-ground cast-iron or steel block with two faces at exactly 90 degrees to each other. It is clamped to a surface plate or machine table to hold a workpiece vertically for layout, drilling, or milling. Slots in the angle plate allow clamps to secure parts of various sizes.

front: What physical hazard classes does WHMIS 2015 recognize?
back: WHMIS 2015 adopted the GHS framework and recognizes 16 physical hazard classes, including: flammable gases, flammable aerosols, oxidizing gases, gases under pressure, flammable liquids, flammable solids, self-reactive substances, pyrophoric liquids and solids, self-heating substances, substances that emit flammable gas on contact with water, oxidizing liquids and solids, organic peroxides, corrosive to metals, desensitized explosives, combustible dusts, and simple asphyxiants. Each class has a distinct GHS pictogram.

front: What health hazard classes does WHMIS 2015 recognize?
back: WHMIS 2015 adopts the GHS framework and recognizes 10 health hazard classes: acute toxicity, skin corrosion and irritation, serious eye damage and eye irritation, respiratory and skin sensitization, germ cell mutagenicity, carcinogenicity, reproductive toxicity, specific target organ toxicity (single exposure), specific target organ toxicity (repeated exposure), and aspiration hazard. Each class has sub-categories rated from Category 1 (most severe) downward.

front: What are the 16 sections of a Safety Data Sheet (SDS)?
back: The 16 sections are: identification; hazard identification; composition; first-aid measures; fire-fighting measures; accidental release; handling and storage; exposure controls and PPE; physical and chemical properties; stability and reactivity; toxicological information; ecological information; disposal; transport; regulatory; and other information. Sections 1 through 8 are the most critical for day-to-day safe handling.

front: What PPE is required for grinding operations in a millwright shop?
back: Grinding requires a face shield (full face protection against flying sparks and particles), safety glasses underneath the face shield, hearing protection (grinding creates high noise levels), leather gloves, and leather or fire-resistant clothing to protect against sparks. Steel-toed boots are always required in the shop. Remove loose clothing or jewelry before grinding.

front: When is a full-face respirator required instead of a half-face respirator?
back: A full-face respirator is required when the contaminant can irritate or damage the eyes as well as the lungs (such as hydrogen sulfide, chlorine, or spray mist), when concentrations exceed the protection factor of a half-face unit, or when eye protection cannot be adequately combined with a half-face mask. The SDS will specify the minimum respiratory protection required.

front: What is the difference between a permit-required and a non-permit confined space?
back: A permit-required confined space has one or more serious hazards: hazardous atmosphere, engulfment risk, converging walls that could trap a person, or any other recognized serious safety hazard. Entry requires a written permit, atmospheric testing, a trained attendant, and a rescue plan. A non-permit space has no such hazards and does not require a formal entry permit.

front: What is the correct atmospheric testing order before confined space entry?
back: Test in this order: first oxygen level (must be 19.5 to 23.5 percent), then combustible/flammable gases (must be below 10 percent of lower explosive limit), then toxic gases such as hydrogen sulfide or carbon monoxide. Testing oxygen first ensures the combustible gas sensor reads accurately, since sensors can fail in low-oxygen environments.

front: List the six steps of lockout/tagout (LOTO) in order.
back: Step 1: identify all energy sources. Step 2: notify affected employees. Step 3: shut down the equipment using normal stopping procedure. Step 4: isolate all energy sources (close valves, open disconnects, block stored energy). Step 5: apply personal locks and tags. Step 6: verify zero energy state by attempting to start and checking pressure gauges and bleed points.

front: What does LOTO verification mean and why must it be done every time?
back: Verification means proving that all energy has been removed and cannot return before you begin work. This includes pressing the start button (and confirming nothing moves), checking that pressure gauges read zero, and confirming that bleed valves remain open. Verification must be done every time because the absence of a lock is not proof that energy is absent.

front: What are the key elements of a hot work permit?
back: A hot work permit identifies the location and type of work (welding, cutting, grinding), lists the combustible materials within the area and the measures taken to protect them (removal, wetting, shielding), requires atmospheric testing results, names the fire watch person and their duties, and states the permit start and expiry time. The fire watch must remain for at least 30 minutes after work ends.

front: What is the minimum anchor point rating for a personal fall arrest system?
back: A personal fall arrest system anchor point must be rated for a minimum of 22.2 kilonewtons (5,000 pounds) per person attached, or be certified by a professional engineer as being able to withstand the maximum arrest force. The anchor must be located above the worker's dorsal D-ring to minimize free fall distance.

front: How do you calculate total fall distance to select a lanyard for fall protection?
back: Total fall distance equals free fall distance (distance fallen before the lanyard engages, maximum 1.8 metres for a standard lanyard) plus deceleration distance (typically 1.2 metres for a shock-absorbing lanyard) plus the worker's height (approximately 1.8 metres from feet to D-ring). Add a safety margin of 0.6 metres. The anchor must provide enough clearance above the landing level.

front: What is the area formula for a triangle and when is it used in the trade?
back: Area of a triangle equals one-half times base times height (A = 0.5 x b x h). Millwrights use this for calculating the cross-sectional area of a V-belt, a triangular gusset plate, or a tapered shim. It also appears when using the 3-4-5 rule for squaring layouts on large foundations.

front: What does the cosine ratio describe in a right triangle?
back: Cosine equals the length of the adjacent side divided by the hypotenuse (CAH). A millwright uses cosine to find the horizontal run of an inclined surface, the horizontal component of a sling load, or the effective bearing width of an angled contact. If the angle is 60 degrees, cosine is 0.500, meaning the horizontal side is half the hypotenuse.

front: How do you calculate the gear ratio of a two-gear mesh from tooth count?
back: Gear ratio equals the number of teeth on the driven gear divided by the number of teeth on the driver gear. A 20-tooth driver meshing with a 60-tooth driven gear gives a ratio of 3:1, meaning the driven gear turns once for every three turns of the driver. Speed and torque change in inverse proportion to the ratio.

front: How do you find the output RPM of a belt drive knowing pulley diameters and input RPM?
back: Output RPM equals input RPM times the ratio of driver pulley diameter to driven pulley diameter. For example, a 6-inch driver turning at 1,800 RPM driving a 9-inch driven pulley gives 1,800 times 6/9, which equals 1,200 RPM. Belt speed stays constant, so the smaller pulley always turns faster than the larger one.

front: What is the volume formula for a sphere and where might a millwright use it?
back: Volume of a sphere equals 4/3 times pi times radius cubed (V = 4/3 x pi x r cubed). A millwright might use this to calculate the capacity of a spherical pressure vessel or tank, or to estimate the weight of a steel ball used in a ball valve. For a 6-inch diameter sphere the radius is 3 inches, giving a volume of about 113 cubic inches.

front: What is a detail view on a drawing and why is it used?
back: A detail view is an enlarged circle or box pulled from a main view to show a small or complex feature at a larger scale with more dimensions. It is labeled (usually with a letter) and the scale is stated separately. Millwrights look for detail views when a keyway, thread, groove, or tight-tolerance feature cannot be clearly dimensioned on the main view.

front: What does a transition fit mean in the context of shaft and bore assembly?
back: A transition fit sits between a clearance fit and an interference fit. Depending on where the actual machined dimensions fall within their tolerances, the assembled pair might have a small clearance or a small interference. Transition fits are used for locating fits where a part must be positioned accurately but still needs to be removable without a press.

front: What does perpendicularity control in GD&T and how is it verified?
back: Perpendicularity controls how much a surface, axis, or line can deviate from being exactly 90 degrees to a datum. It is verified by placing the part against the datum surface on a surface plate and measuring the deviation from 90 degrees with a dial indicator swept along the controlled surface. Tight perpendicularity is critical for bearing housings and mating flanges.

front: What does parallelism control in GD&T and when is it important for a millwright?
back: Parallelism controls how much a surface or axis can deviate from being exactly parallel to a datum. It is important for machine bed ways, linear guide rails, and shaft mounting pads where non-parallel surfaces cause binding, uneven loading, or misalignment. It is measured with a dial indicator swept across the surface while the part rests on the datum reference.

front: What is concentricity in GD&T and how does it differ from runout?
back: Concentricity controls whether the median points of a feature (the centre points of cross-sections) all lie within a cylindrical tolerance zone centred on a datum axis. Runout controls the surface directly and is much easier to measure with a dial indicator. In practice, runout is almost always specified instead of concentricity because it is simpler to verify.

front: What is the angularity GD&T symbol used to control?
back: Angularity controls a surface or axis that is at a specified angle other than 0 or 90 degrees to a datum. The tolerance zone is two parallel planes (or a cylinder) at the exact nominal angle to the datum. It is used for angled mounting faces, beveled surfaces, and inclined bores where the angle is critical for mating part alignment.

front: What does the position GD&T symbol control on a pattern of holes?
back: The position symbol controls how far the centre of a hole (or other feature) can be from its theoretically exact location. The tolerance zone is a cylinder centred on the true position, and the hole axis must stay inside that cylinder. It is the most commonly used GD&T control for bolt patterns, pin locations, and any feature that must line up with a mating part.

front: What is the difference between IWRC and fibre core wire rope and when is each used?
back: IWRC (independent wire rope core) has a small wire rope at its centre, giving it about 7.5 percent higher breaking strength and better resistance to crushing under heavy loads. Fibre core wire rope has a synthetic or natural fibre centre that acts as a lubricant reservoir, making it more flexible but less crush-resistant. Use IWRC for overhead lifting and running lines; fibre core is better for standing rigging where flexibility matters more than crush resistance.

front: What is the difference between regular lay and lang lay wire rope?
back: In regular lay wire rope, the wires in each strand are twisted opposite to the direction the strands are twisted around the core, which makes the rope resist rotation and is most common for lifting. In lang lay, both the wires and the strands are twisted in the same direction, giving better fatigue resistance and abrasion resistance but making the rope more prone to rotation under load.

front: What are the wire rope discard criteria based on broken wires per lay length?
back: Discard a wire rope if it has six or more randomly distributed broken wires in one rope lay length, or three or more broken wires in one strand in one lay length. A lay length is approximately 6.5 times the rope diameter. These criteria apply to running ropes; standing ropes may have different discard thresholds per the manufacturer and applicable standard.

front: What other wire rope conditions require immediate removal from service?
back: Remove a wire rope if it shows kinking, birdcaging (strands pushed apart), heat damage (discolouration, brittleness), corrosion pitting on the outer wires, a reduction in diameter of more than 3 percent from nominal, or core protrusion. Any one of these conditions makes the rope unsafe even if the broken-wire count is within limits.

front: What is the purpose of a swivel in a rigging assembly and when should it not be used?
back: A swivel allows the load to rotate freely without transmitting torque to the wire rope or chain, preventing twist buildup in the rigging. However, a swivel must never be used in a way that allows the load line to unscrew the swivel jaw under load. Also, do not use a plain swivel with lang lay wire rope, as it will unlay the rope and reduce strength.

front: How does the angle of an eyebolt reduce its rated load capacity?
back: An eyebolt is rated at full capacity only when the load is applied in line with the shank (straight pull). At 45 degrees from the shank axis, capacity drops to 50 percent of rated load. At 90 degrees (pulling sideways on the eye), capacity drops to 25 percent. Always use shoulder pattern eyebolts for angular loads, never plain pattern eyebolts.

front: What are the 11 standard crane hand signals a signal person must know?
back: The 11 standard ASME/CSA crane hand signals are: hoist, lower, use main hoist, use whip line, bridge travel (both directions), trolley travel (both directions), stop, emergency stop, dog everything, and move slowly. The signal person must have clear visual contact with the operator at all times, and the operator follows only the designated signal person's directions.

front: What are the three levels of overhead crane inspection and their frequency?
back: Pre-use inspection is performed by the operator at the start of each shift and checks hooks, chains or wire rope, limit switches, brakes, and controls. Periodic inspection is monthly to quarterly depending on service class and checks structural members, fasteners, and electrical components. Annual (frequent and periodic combined) is a full documented inspection covering all components by a qualified person.

front: What is the difference between proof load and working load limit (WLL) for rigging hardware?
back: Working load limit (WLL) is the maximum load a piece of hardware is designed to carry in normal service. Proof load is the test load applied during manufacturing to verify the hardware will not deform or fail; it is typically twice the WLL for most hardware. Proof load is not a usable working load; it is a one-time factory quality check.

front: How does sling angle affect the tension in each leg of a two-leg bridle sling?
back: As the sling angle from the horizontal decreases (legs become more spread), the tension in each leg increases dramatically for the same vertical load. At 60 degrees from horizontal each leg carries 1.15 times the load per leg. At 45 degrees it is 1.41 times. At 30 degrees it is 2.0 times. Never rig with a sling angle below 30 degrees from horizontal.

front: What is the de-rating factor for a wire rope sling in a choker hitch versus a straight pull?
back: A wire rope sling in a choker hitch has a rated capacity of approximately 75 percent (0.75 times) of its straight vertical hitch rating, because the bend over the load concentrates stress on the wire rope and fitting. A basket hitch with both legs vertical doubles the capacity to 2.0 times the straight hitch rating.

front: How does a basket hitch sling angle affect the working load limit?
back: A basket hitch with both legs at 90 degrees (straight down) gives a WLL of 2.0 times the single-leg vertical rating. As the legs spread and the sling angle decreases, the WLL drops. At 60 degrees from horizontal the efficiency factor is 1.73. At 45 degrees it is 1.41. At 30 degrees it falls to 1.0, equal to a single vertical leg.

front: What is a spreader bar (equalizer beam) used for in rigging and what problem does it solve?
back: A spreader bar (or equalizer beam) is a rigid bar or beam suspended from the crane hook with slings attached at each end to lift long or fragile loads. It prevents the slings from squeezing the load inward as they angle toward the hook, distributes the load evenly across multiple pick points, and allows vertical sling legs even when the pick points are far apart.

front: What is the difference between a tugger and a come-along for moving loads horizontally?
back: A come-along (hand-operated ratchet lever hoist) is a manual tool used for light pulling or positioning loads, typically up to 3 tonnes, using lever action and a hand chain. A tugger is a powered drum hoist (electric or pneumatic) mounted to a fixed structure or crane that provides much higher line pull for moving heavy loads horizontally. Both require proper rigging and anchor points rated for the load.

front: What is the difference between a chain hoist and a chain fall and what are their uses?
back: A chain hoist (lever hoist) is operated by moving a lever back and forth and is used for tensioning, positioning, and pulling loads in any direction. A chain fall (chain block) is operated by pulling the hand chain and is designed primarily for vertical lifting only. Both use mechanical advantage through a gear reduction to multiply force, and both are rated with a WLL that must not be exceeded.

front: What are the safe working rules for a bottle (hydraulic) jack when lifting machinery?
back: Always place the jack on a firm, level surface. Never exceed the jack's rated capacity. Use hardwood or steel blocking under the jack base and under the load to spread the load and prevent sinking. Keep the ram extension within the manufacturer's limits (never extend past the safety collar). Always secure the load with blocking before working under it, as a jack is not a safe hold.

front: How do you use a jacking beam to lift a load that has no single central jack point?
back: A jacking beam is a structural beam placed under the load at two or more support points. Jacks push up on the jacking beam, which distributes the lift to multiple load contact points simultaneously. This prevents point loading damage to equipment bases, allows a load to be raised evenly without tilting, and is essential when lifting equipment over a long span.

front: What is the correct procedure for skidding a heavy machine using steel rollers?
back: Place steel pipe rollers under the machine skid or base plate (typically three or more rollers perpendicular to the direction of travel). Push the load with a come-along or chain fall, feeding the last roller from the rear to the front as the machine moves forward. Keep rollers parallel and evenly spaced. The floor must be clean, flat, and able to carry the load without cracking.

front: What is the stability triangle of a forklift and why does it matter?
back: The forklift stability triangle is the area between the two front drive wheels and the single rear steer axle pivot point. The combined centre of gravity of the forklift and its load must stay inside this triangle for the forklift to remain stable. Overloading, raising a load too high, or turning sharply moves the centre of gravity outside the triangle, causing a tip-over.

front: When are personnel allowed to ride in the forks or on a load of a forklift?
back: Personnel are generally prohibited from riding on the forks or on a load unless a purpose-built, rated work platform is securely attached to the forks per the manufacturer's instructions and applicable safety regulations. Even with an approved platform, the forklift must travel at walking speed and the operator must not leave the controls. Never use forks directly as an improvised man-lift.

front: What is the minimum safe clearance required from overhead power lines during crane operations?
back: Under most Canadian and provincial regulations, a minimum clearance of 3 metres (approximately 10 feet) is required from overhead power lines up to 75 kV. For higher voltages the clearance increases. Always contact the utility owner before beginning any lift near power lines. The safest approach is to have the utility de-energize the line before the lift.

front: What is a lift plan and when is one required before a crane pick?
back: A lift plan is a written document that describes the load weight and dimensions, the crane or hoist to be used, rigging configuration and hardware with WLLs confirmed, the pick and set-down points, ground bearing capacity, swing radius exclusion zones, and the signal person and rigging crew assignments. A formal lift plan is required for critical lifts (near capacity, over personnel, tandem crane picks) and is best practice for all non-routine lifts.

front: What is a shackle and what are the two main types used in rigging?
back: A shackle is a U-shaped steel rigging connector with a removable pin used to attach slings, blocks, and hardware. The two main types are the anchor (omega) shackle, which handles in-line and angular loads well, and the chain (D) shackle, which has a narrower bow and is used where the load is applied in-line only. Screw-pin shackles must have the pin moused or safety-wired when used in a running block.

front: What is a turnbuckle used for in rigging and what is its load rating rule?
back: A turnbuckle is a threaded tensioning device used to adjust the length and tension of a wire rope, chain, or rod. It has a left-hand thread on one end and a right-hand thread on the other so turning the body shortens or lengthens the assembly. The WLL is stamped on the body. Never use a turnbuckle as a primary load-bearing sling; it is a tensioning and adjustment device.

front: What is a hoist ring (swivel hoist ring) and why is it preferred over a plain eyebolt?
back: A hoist ring is a threaded lifting point with a bail that pivots and swivels in all directions to stay aligned with the sling regardless of lift angle, maintaining full rated capacity at any angle. A plain eyebolt drops to 25 to 30 percent capacity at 90 degrees. Hoist rings are preferred for lifting machinery that requires angular picks or where the direction of pull is not straight up through the shank.

front: What is right-hand lay wire rope and how is it identified on site?
back: Right-hand lay wire rope has its strands twisted clockwise (to the right) when you look along the rope away from you, like a right-hand screw thread. It is the most common type used in industry. To identify it, hold the rope vertically: if the strands slope upward to the right, it is right-hand lay. Left-hand lay is used in special applications such as multi-part reeving to counteract torque.

front: How do you determine the centre of gravity of an asymmetric load before rigging?
back: For an asymmetric load, use the manufacturer's drawing if available since it will often mark the centre of gravity. If not, balance test: lift slightly off the ground with a single pick and observe which end drops. Shift the pick point toward the heavy end until the load hangs level. Mark the balance point and confirm all rigging hardware is rated for the full load at that configuration.

front: What is the purpose of a tag line during a crane lift and who controls it?
back: A tag line is a rope (never wire rope) attached to the load to control rotation and prevent the load from swinging into structures or personnel during travel. It is controlled by a designated ground worker who keeps tension on it while walking alongside the moving load. The tag line must never be wrapped around hands or body parts; hold it only in the hands with a clear release path.

front: What is a pick plan and how does it differ from a lift plan?
back: A pick plan is the portion of a lift plan that focuses specifically on the rigging configuration: how the slings attach to the load, the attachment points, sling angles, hardware selected, and the WLL confirmation for each component. A lift plan is broader and includes the crane selection, ground conditions, swing path, crew roles, and emergency procedures. The pick plan is a subset of the full lift plan.

front: What inspection must be performed on a chain hoist before every use?
back: Pre-use inspection includes checking the load chain for twisted, stretched, cracked, or worn links (discard if any link is worn more than 10 percent of original diameter). Check the hook for cracks, deformation, or a damaged safety latch. Confirm the brake engages and holds under a test lift. Check that the hand chain is intact and moves freely. Tag and remove from service any hoist that fails inspection.

front: How do you rig a choker hitch on a cylindrical load such as a shaft or pipe?
back: Pass one end of the sling around the load and through the other end (or through the choker fitting), then attach the free end to the hook. The choker must grip the load at least 30 degrees from the bottom (the self-tightening angle). Do not place the choke point at a sharp corner or edge without using a corner protector, as edges can cut the sling under load.

front: What is the maximum number of degrees a shackle pin can be loaded off the straight line of pull?
back: A shackle should be loaded in the plane of the bow (straight through the pin axis). Side loading a shackle pin, where the pin is loaded at an angle to its axis, dramatically reduces its capacity and can cause the bow to distort and the pin to walk out. Where angular loads are unavoidable, use an appropriately rated anchor shackle and stay within the manufacturer's angular de-rating guidance.

front: What does mousing a hook mean and when is it required?
back: Mousing a hook means securing the safety latch with wire or a tie strap so it cannot accidentally open under the sling. It is required when there is any risk that vibration, side loading, or contact with the load could pop the latch open and release the sling. Standard practice in most jurisdictions requires mousing on all lifting hooks unless a self-closing, self-locking safety latch is fitted.

front: What is the safe-working rule for loading the tip of a crane hook?
back: A crane hook must never be tip-loaded (loaded at the very tip of the hook) because this concentrates stress at the weakest point and can straighten the hook open. The load must seat at the saddle (the deepest inside bend of the hook). Always size your rigging hardware so the load seats correctly and does not slide toward the tip under load.

front: How do dollies differ from rollers when moving heavy machinery?
back: Rollers are simple steel pipes placed under a skid and moved one at a time as the load travels forward. Dollies are wheeled platforms (steel or polyurethane wheels) that stay attached to the machine for the entire move, allowing steering and direction changes that rollers cannot provide. Dollies are faster and give more control but require a flat, hard floor and sufficient clearance under the machine base.

front: What does the term safe working load (SWL) mean compared to WLL?
back: Safe working load (SWL) is an older term meaning the same thing as working load limit (WLL): the maximum load a piece of equipment is designed to handle in normal service. WLL is the current preferred term in most Canadian and international standards. Both values already include the manufacturer's design safety factor; the operator must never exceed either without written engineering approval.

front: What is a tandem lift and what additional precautions does it require?
back: A tandem lift uses two cranes simultaneously to lift a single load that is too large or heavy for one crane. It requires a lift director coordinating both operators, a written lift plan with load distribution calculations for each crane, communication protocol between operators (radio), and both cranes must be rated for their share of the load including all dynamic factors. Tandem lifts are classified as critical lifts in all jurisdictions.

front: What are the main components of a wire rope end termination using a swaged socket?
back: A swaged (mechanical) socket termination consists of a steel socket with a tapered cavity and a steel ferrule. The rope end is inserted, the wires are spread or the ferrule is positioned, and a hydraulic press swages (compresses) the metal around the rope to form a permanent, full-strength connection rated at 100 percent of the rope's minimum breaking force. It cannot be inspected internally once installed and must be discarded if any cracking or distortion is found on the socket.

front: What is the correct way to store wire rope slings after use to extend their service life?
back: Clean the sling to remove dirt, grit, and corrosive materials. Lightly oil the wire rope to prevent corrosion. Hang slings on a rack (not piled on the floor) so they drain and dry. Store in a clean, dry area away from chemicals, heat, and direct sunlight. Inspect before storage and tag any sling that needs repair so it is not accidentally returned to service.

front: What information must appear on a rigging inspection tag attached to a sling?
back: A rigging inspection tag must show the sling identification number, the rated WLL for each hitch type, the date of last inspection, the name or initials of the inspector, and the next inspection due date. Any sling without a current valid inspection tag must be removed from service until inspected and re-tagged. This documentation requirement applies to wire rope, chain, and synthetic web slings.
